content.title: Undo Without Panic
content.hook: “Undo this” is not a precise request.
content.context:
Consider four situations:

1. You edited a file but have not staged it.
2. You staged a file but have not committed it.
3. You committed the change locally.
4. You pushed the commit to a shared remote.

The safest recovery depends on which state you are in.
goals: Distinguish common kinds of Git mistakes and choose a recovery strategy based on whether the change is unstaged, staged, committed locally, or already shared.

content.title: State matters
content.text:
Use this investigation sequence:

```text
git status
   ↓
Did I stage it?
   ↓
Did I commit it?
   ↓
Did I push it?
```

The point is to find the smallest safe intervention.

content.title: Unstaged mistake
content.text:
You accidentally changed `styles.css` and want to discard the local change.

Before doing anything destructive, confirm what changed.

The important lesson is not a single command.

The lesson is:

> **Do not destroy work before you have identified exactly what state you are in and what you intend to preserve.**

content.question:
You committed a bad change locally.

You have not shared it yet.

What should guide your next decision?

options.text: The fact that a commit exists means it can never be changed.
Whether you need to preserve the history exactly as recorded or create a corrected history before sharing.
Whether the commit message has the right emoji.

feedback.correct: Local history gives you recovery options. Shared history needs more care because other people may depend on it.
feedback.incorrect: Local history gives you recovery options. Shared history needs more care because other people may depend on it.

content.question:
A bad commit has already been pushed and teammates may have based work on it.

What principle should dominate?

options.text: Rewrite shared history immediately without telling anyone.
Prefer a recovery strategy that makes the correction understandable to collaborators and avoids silently invalidating their history.
Pretend the commit does not exist.

feedback.correct: Once history is shared, the impact is social as well as technical.
feedback.incorrect: Once history is shared, the impact is social as well as technical.

content.title: The safest habit
content.text:
When something goes wrong:

**Stop. Inspect. Identify the state. Choose the smallest recovery. Verify.**

That sequence is more valuable than memorizing twenty undo commands.

content.question:
A teammate asks:

> “Can you undo my last change?”

What is the first question you should ask?

feedback.correct: Shared vs local history changes what recovery strategy is safe.
feedback.incorrect: Shared vs local history changes what recovery strategy is safe.

content.title: Forge takeaway & Lesson completion
takeaways: **Senior habit:** Never run a destructive command just because you remember the command. First identify the state you are trying to change.
